'''Peter Michael Rentzepis''' (born 11 December 1934) is a Greek-born American physical chemist.

== Education and career ==
Rentzepis is a native of [[Kalamata]] born on 11 December 1934.<ref>''American Men and Women of Science'', Thomson Gale 2004.</ref> Rentzepis attended the 1st Lykion in his hometown and graduated from [[Denison University]] and [[Syracuse University]] in the United States before pursuing a doctorate at the [[University of Cambridge]] in the United Kingdom, graduating in 1963.<ref name="mqww">{{cite journal |title=Peter M. Rentzepis |journal=Marquis Who's Who Top Educators |date=20 September 2017 |url=https://marquistopeducators.com/2017/09/20/peter-m-rentzepis/ |archive-date=19 December 2018 |access-date=18 December 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181219001241/https://marquistopeducators.com/2017/09/20/peter-m-rentzepis/ |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name="tolman">{{cite news |title=2001 Peter M. Rentzepis, UC Irvine |url=https://scalacs.org/?page_id=1093 |access-date=18 December 2018 |publisher=Southern California Section of the American Physical Society}}</ref> Rentzepis, who joined Bell Labs in 1963, after two years at [[General Electric]],<ref>{{cite news |title=Peter M. Rentzepis |url=http://energy.tamu.edu/faculty-experts/peter-m-rentzepis/ |access-date=18 December 2018 |publisher=Texas A&M University |archive-date=19 December 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181219042440/http://energy.tamu.edu/faculty-experts/peter-m-rentzepis/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> led the physical and inorganic chemistry research department at Bell between 1973 and 1985, and taught at the [[University of California, Irvine]] from 1974 to 2014,<ref name="mqww"/> serving in a presidential chair professorship from 1985.<ref name="tolman"/>  In 2014, Rentzepis was appointed TEES Distinguished Professor at [[Texas A&M University]].<ref name="mqww"/> While at the university, he submitted an application in 1989 and published after patents (US5268862A<ref>{{Cite web |title=US-5268862-A - Patent Public Search {{!}} USPTO |url=https://ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/patents/html/5268862?source=USPAT&requestToken=eyJzdWIiOiI2ZWVjZjU5Mi0yNDE1LTQwMTktYTc1Ny1iMDkwZWZiNjdjYWMiLCJ2ZXIiOiJiOGIxMGRiOC03N2U0LTRiYTItOTY2OS1jNjI0ZGQ3NGVlMDAiLCJleHAiOjB9 |access-date=2024-10-22 |website=ppubs.uspto.gov}}</ref> & US5325324A<ref>{{Cite web |title=US-5325324-A - Patent Public Search {{!}} USPTO |url=https://ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/patents/html/5325324?source=USPAT&requestToken=eyJzdWIiOiI2ZWVjZjU5Mi0yNDE1LTQwMTktYTc1Ny1iMDkwZWZiNjdjYWMiLCJ2ZXIiOiJiOGIxMGRiOC03N2U0LTRiYTItOTY2OS1jNjI0ZGQ3NGVlMDAiLCJleHAiOjB9 |access-date=2024-10-22 |website=ppubs.uspto.gov}}</ref> - Three-dimensional optical memory) approval in 1994. The research was conducted under grant No. F30602-97-C-0014 between the United States Air Force (USAF) acting through its Office of Special Research (AFOSR) and The Regents of the University of California.

== Honors and awards ==
Rentzepis was elected a fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] in 1972,<ref>{{cite news |title=APS Fellow Archive |url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=R&year=&unit_id=&institution= |access-date=18 December 2018 |publisher=American Physical Society}}</ref> and a member of the [[United States National Academy of Sciences]] in 1978.<ref>{{cite news |title=60 scientists named to national academy |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1978/04/30/archives/60-scientists-named-to-national-academy-selection-is-high-honor.html |access-date=18 December 2018 |work=The New York Times|date=30 April 1978}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Peter M. Rentzepis |url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/peter-m-rentzepis-gyrirj/ |access-date=18 December 2018 |publisher=United States National Academy of Sciences}}</ref> He won the 1982 [[Peter Debye Award]] from the [[American Chemical Society]],<ref>{{cite news |title=Peter Debye Award in Physical Chemistry |url=https://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/funding-and-awards/awards/national/bytopic/peter-debye-award-in-physical-chemistry.html |access-date=18 December 2018 |publisher=American Chemical Society}}</ref> followed in 1989 by the [[Irving Langmuir Award]] from the [[American Physical Society]],<ref>{{cite journal |title=American Physical Society presents awards to four |journal=Physics Today |date=1973 |volume=24 |issue=6 |page=69 |doi=10.1063/1.3128026}}</ref> and in 2001 by the [[Tolman Award]] of the ACS Southern California Section.<ref name="tolman"/>
